old: It began as a word for a simple wooden frame you'd sleep on, carried into English from a language of South Asia.
Its ancestor is the Sanskrit word khaṭvā, meaning bedstead.
It arrived in English by way of Hindi khāṭ, naming a portable bed.
clues: This piece of furniture was borrowed into English from Hindi, and its roots reach back to an ancient Sanskrit word for a wooden bedstead.
It is a narrow, lightweight bed, often folding, set up in camps, barracks or hospitals, and simpler and more portable than an ordinary bed or bunk.
In Britain it also means a baby's barred crib, and an unrelated twin word from Old English once named a small, humble dwelling.
